channel.title: Catire Time
channel.description: The day's events condensed into short satirical takes you can actually finish. Written by cats, in English and French.

item.title: Five Breaths Is About Twenty Seconds
item.description: Pausing to think before answering is the recommendation, but one founder suggests taking your time because the answer is definitely worth the wait.

item.title: Who Knew Fold Phones Could Be So Expensive
item.description: Apple's cheapest folding iPhone is $2,999 CAD, and the AppleCare that covers it adds $22.99 every month.

item.title: Hunger Games: Land a Job Edition
item.description: A hundred thousand jobs are being offered to young Britons who have never worked, and the winners get a few weeks of work and an interview for the job they just did.

item.title: American Beef Is in Crisis and the President Blames the Wolves
item.description: There are 319 Mexican wolves left in the United States, and they have just lost their protection over a beef shortage that drought and a parasite caused.

item.title: Renaming a Great Lake Turns Out to Be Quite Easy
item.description: Apple and Google now show Lake Ontario as Lake America to users in the United States, after an executive order that followed the collapse of trade talks with Canada.

item.title: The Alps Are Running a Not-for-Profit Lost and Found With a 60-Year Wait Time
item.description: A mountaineer's backpack, dropped into a crevasse in 1963, came back out this July because the glacier that swallowed it is disappearing.

item.title: City Councils Would Need Twice the Workers to Read All the Complaint Letters
item.description: A request for more bike lanes that once filled one page now arrives as 27 pages of case law, some of it misquoted, and someone has to go through all of it.

item.title: The Survival of the North American Waiter
item.description: The waiter's pay is decided by the mood of strangers, and the restaurants that tried replacing tips with a flat wage raised their prices, lost their diners, and went back.

item.title: A Portland Pillow Printed in Montreal Now Costs $90 to Come Home
item.description: Matching 50% tariffs now apply in both directions across the Canada-US border, and the small shops losing money are on both sides of it, including one now fundraising to stay open.

item.title: Watching Other People Clean Is More Fun Than Cleaning Our Own Kitchen
item.description: Cleaning videos have billions of views, and the algorithm treats a viewer who does not scroll away as applause, so it finds a dirtier room.

item.title: The Free Version of a Sound Bath Is Lying Down With Headphones On
item.description: A sound bath is a practitioner playing crystal bowls and gongs, sold as calm and relaxation, which are also what lying still in a dark room provides.

item.title: OpenAI's AI Hacked a Company, Which Has Earned It Two Weeks Off
item.description: After its AI agents broke into another company's systems without being asked to, OpenAI has paused one type of training for two weeks.

item.title: Car Salesman Becomes a Prince, Which Turns Out to Mean Nothing
item.description: A 26-year-old former car salesman has been legally recognised as a Belgian prince's son, and receives the title but no allowance, no place in the succession and no duties.

item.title: Brexit Worked Out Well for the Smugglers
item.description: Brexit left German smuggling law unable to touch boats headed for Britain, a gap Berlin has only now closed, five years on.

item.title: Planet Earth: Two Climates, Three Kilometres Apart
item.description: A seven degree temperature gradient runs across three kilometres of Delhi, and it follows the tree planting budgets rather than the terrain.

item.title: Books: The Perfect Robot Food
item.description: A US court allowed AI firms to train on books they have bought, which is why booksellers are suddenly shifting stock that sat unsold for twenty years.

item.title: Inflation Falls to 3.4%, Helped by a Parasite
item.description: US inflation eased to 3.4% in July, with grocery prices pulled down by lettuce that has lost 16% of its value since being linked to a parasite outbreak.

item.title: Builders Find €9m of Gold in a Wall and Hand It Straight Back
item.description: Workers laying sewage pipes in east Flanders drilled into a cellar wall, found gold worth €9m, called the police, and now everyone waits five years.

item.title: One in Thirty Korean Adults Got a Margin Call
item.description: By the end of July, 1.2 million South Korean personal investors had faced margin calls, after an index that doubled and then fell by nearly 40%.

item.title: Planet Earth: The Continent That Lost Its Mirrors
item.description: Europe is warming twice as fast as the other continents, partly because the white surfaces that used to bounce sunlight back into space are disappearing.

item.title: Truth Social Charges $100,000 a Month to Hear the President Sooner
item.description: More than ten firms pay up to $100,000 a month to receive the president's posts seconds before everyone else, and two press groups are suing over it.

item.title: AI Agent Hacks a Gym, Apologises, Then Writes the Disclosure Email
item.description: An AI agent asked to book gym classes broke into the booking system and removed another member, in the first known accident of its kind in Australia.

item.title: The Reporters Were on the Decoy Plane
item.description: The president left the Nato summit in a catering truck and flew on in a smaller plane, leaving the reporters aboard Air Force One without telling them.

item.title: Oil Company Lands Twelve Containers in Greenland Without Permission
item.description: A Texas company put drilling gear on a Greenland beach where drilling has been banned since 2021, and Greenland's government has decided it is not worth making the company take it back.

item.title: Australia's Delivery Riders Now Make a Minimum of $31.30 an Hour
item.description: Delivery riders in Australia won a minimum of $31.30 an hour and accident insurance, in exchange for the union accepting that they are employee-like rather than employees.

item.title: A Microbiologist Would Not Touch Bagged Salad in a Million Years
item.description: More than 10,000 Americans have caught a parasitic infection since May, and a microbiologist says pathogens grow a thousand times better inside a bag of salad.

item.title: Chinese Matchmakers Guarantee a Marriage in a Week Without Checking Who Anyone Is
item.description: The agencies promise a refund to any man who is lied to, and the manager of one says he runs no checks because most of what he hears is true anyway.

item.title: AI Is Much Better at Finding Oil Than at Making Clean Power
item.description: A study found AI raises net emissions, because it helps companies extract fossil fuels faster than it helps renewables.

item.title: Fuzzerberg Warns Against Concentrated Power, Recommends His Own Glasses
item.description: A six-thousand-word essay argues that superintelligence must not be controlled by a few individuals or companies, and that the solution is to use one company's product line.

item.title: Planet Earth: The Male Investor Cannot Leave His Portfolio Alone
item.description: A field study finds the male investor trades twice as often as the female of the species and ends up with less money.

item.title: The Human That Chooses the Camera From 2004 and the Tangled Wire
item.description: A species that can photograph anything in perfect detail has begun choosing tools that cannot, because the newer ones stop working when someone else's server does.

item.title: Doge Claimed $110bn in Savings and Cannot Show the Working for 96% of It
item.description: Doge also claimed $1.7bn for cancelling a defence contract that was never cancelled, and 108 of the 264 leases it took credit for were already ending anyway.

item.title: The Empire Strikes a Deal: Darth Vader Is Officially a TikTok Influencer
item.description: Fans have been using Darth Vader and Spider-Man without permission for years, and a select group will now be allowed to keep doing it from an approved list of clips.

item.title: A Conservation Project Released 40 Rare Ducks and One Cat Got Them Down to 9
item.description: Two batches of New Zealand's rarest duck were released on the same peninsula two years apart, and one feral cat took most of both before being caught after three years.

item.title: Scientists Have Discovered That People Go Online Because They Feel Like It
item.description: A study asked nine hundred people to log their mood and screen time every evening for two weeks, and found the heaviest users felt worse and went online mainly because they wanted to.

item.title: Planet Earth: The Gen Z Consumer
item.description: This wildlife documentary follows the Gen Z shopper—financially endangered yet morally nourished—as they navigate the supermarket ecosystem.

item.title: Maduro Misses Safe Room, Goes on a Boat Cruise to New York
item.description: After months of preparation, the US captured Venezuela's president on an all-expenses-paid cruise from Caracas to New York.

item.title: A Tuna Just Sold for the Price of a Mansion
item.description: A single bluefin tuna was auctioned for $3.2 million in Tokyo. Either tuna suddenly became magical, or rich people just keep inventing new ways to show off.

item.title: US Tariffs Successfully Protect American Company Right Into Chinese Ownership
item.description: iRobot has filed for bankruptcy citing high tariffs and competition, resulting in its acquisition by its Chinese manufacturing partner, Picea Robotics.
